title: Build serverless AI backends with Azure Functions

questions.q: A new serverless AI backend should scale to zero for most functions but keep the chat endpoint warm. Which plan does Learn recommend?

options.why: Legacy Linux Consumption retires after September 2028.
Correct. Always-ready keeps chosen functions warm while others scale to zero.

options.text: Premium with one pre-warmed worker for every function
options.why: Premium keeps workers always running; you pay the always-on cost.
Dedicated makes sense when spare App Service capacity exists.

questions.hint: The recommended default plan for new apps can keep a few instances warm.
questions.explain: Flex Consumption is the recommended default for new serverless apps.

questions.q: What is the HTTP trigger timeout imposed by the Azure Load Balancer?

options.why: functionTimeout can't extend the load balancer limit.
Correct. HTTP-triggered functions time out after 230 seconds.
Service Bus triggers can be unbounded on Flex and Premium; HTTP can't.
30 seconds is Event Grid's response wait.

questions.hint: The load balancer cuts HTTP calls off after a fixed time, whatever the plan.
questions.explain: Long work → async request-reply with a Service Bus-triggered function.

questions.q: Document extraction takes 6–8 minutes per file and is started by an HTTP call. Which design does Learn recommend?

options.text: Return 200 after 220 seconds and keep working in the same call
options.why: The client never gets the result, and the work isn't decoupled.

options.text: Queue it to Service Bus, return 202, process in a queue-triggered function
options.why: Correct. Async request-reply avoids the 230-second HTTP limit.

options.text: Raise functionTimeout in host.json to 10 minutes for the app
options.why: The load balancer limit applies regardless of functionTimeout.

options.text: Move to Premium so that HTTP calls can run for 10 minutes
options.why: The 230-second limit applies on every plan.

questions.hint: Long work started over HTTP must not keep the HTTP call open.
questions.explain: Decouple ingestion from processing so each scales on its own.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A Flex Consumption app has two HTTP functions, a Service Bus trigger and a timer trigger.

rows.text: The two HTTP functions scale together on the same instances.
rows.why: All HTTP triggers scale together as a group.

rows.text: A surge of Service Bus messages competes with HTTP requests on the same instances.
rows.why: Non-HTTP triggers scale on their own independent instances.

rows.text: Choosing 4,096 MB instances gives each instance 2 vCPUs.
rows.why: CPU scales with memory: 4,096 MB = 2 vCPU.

rows.text: The app can run on Windows if needed.

questions.hint: Per-function scaling groups HTTP triggers together. Memory size sets the vCPUs.
questions.explain: Per-function scaling isolates trigger types; instance size sets memory and CPU.

questions.q: Inference functions need a GPU and custom OS-level packages, and must run next to other containerized microservices. Which hosting option fits?

options.why: Flex Consumption doesn't provide GPUs.
Dedicated is for reusing spare App Service capacity.
Correct. Container Apps hosting suits GPU access, custom OS packages and side-by-side containers.
Premium supports custom images but Learn points to Container Apps for GPU.

questions.hint: GPU and custom OS packages next to other containers.
questions.explain: Pick Container Apps when functions need GPU or custom OS packages.

questions.q: A Flex Consumption function loads a large model and needs two vCPUs and stable per-call performance. What should you choose?

options.text: 2,048 MB instances with always-ready instances set
options.why: Always-ready avoids cold starts, but each instance still has 1 vCPU.

options.text: 512 MB instances with many more instances
options.why: Small instances don't give two vCPUs to one invocation.
Correct. 4,096 MB gives 2 vCPUs, and lower concurrency gives each invocation more dedicated resources.
2,048 MB gives 1 vCPU, and higher concurrency makes invocations share it.

questions.hint: CPU grows with instance memory, and concurrency decides how many calls share an instance.
questions.explain: Flex Consumption instance sizes are 512, 2,048 and 4,096 MB; CPU scales with memory (4,096 MB = 2 vCPUs). Lower concurrency spreads load across more instances and isolates resources per invocation.

questions.q: A team is starting a new Linux function app and plans to use the Consumption plan because their older apps use it. What should you tell them?

options.text: Linux Consumption is still the recommended default for new apps
options.why: Flex Consumption is the recommended default for new serverless apps.

options.text: It's a legacy plan retiring in 2028; use Flex Consumption
options.why: Correct. New projects should use Flex Consumption.

options.text: Linux Consumption is fine, because it now supports always-ready instances
options.why: Always-ready instances are a Flex Consumption feature.

options.text: Use the Dedicated plan, because serverless plans don't run Python
options.why: Serverless plans run Python. The issue is the legacy plan.

questions.hint: One of the serverless plans is being retired.
questions.explain: The Linux Consumption plan is legacy; running function apps on Linux in a Consumption plan retires after September 2028. New projects should use Flex Consumption.

questions.q: You run a function app locally with Core Tools. At which address are HTTP triggers exposed by default?

options.why: Correct. Core Tools exposes HTTP endpoints on port 7071 by default.
5000 isn't the Functions default.
443 isn't used locally by Core Tools.
10000 is the Azure Managed Redis port.

questions.hint: Core Tools runs the host on localhost with a default port.
questions.explain: func start or F5 launches the host on localhost:7071.

questions.q: Locally, HTTP functions work but a queue trigger and a timer trigger never fire. AzureWebJobsStorage is empty. What should you set?

options.why: Correct. The runtime needs storage for non-HTTP triggers; Azurite emulates it locally.

options.text: A Cosmos DB emulator connection string
options.why: Cosmos DB isn't the runtime's storage dependency.
The worker runtime isn't the missing piece here.
Timeouts don't make triggers fire.

questions.hint: Non-HTTP triggers need a storage connection, even locally.
questions.explain: Without a valid storage connection, non-HTTP triggers don't work.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A team sets up a Python Functions project in VS Code.

rows.text: local.settings.json should be committed so teammates get the same secrets.
rows.why: Never commit it; it often contains secrets.

rows.text: The .vscode folder should be committed for a consistent F5 experience.
rows.why: Learn says to commit these files.

rows.text: func init and func new also generate the .vscode configuration files.
rows.why: They don't; use Create Function... or add them manually.

rows.text: Changes in host.json affect every function in the app.

questions.hint: Commit code and editor config. Keep local secrets out of Git.
questions.explain: Commit code and editor config; keep local secrets out of source control.

questions.q: You fetched production settings into local.settings.json with Core Tools and now worry about secrets on your laptop. What does Learn suggest?

options.why: Correct. Core Tools encrypts the file; only Core Tools on the same machine can decrypt it.
Renaming doesn't protect the values.

options.text: Set IsEncrypted to true by hand
options.why: Editing the flag doesn't encrypt the values.

options.text: Commit the file to a private repository
options.why: Committing secrets is exactly what to avoid.

questions.hint: Core Tools has a command that protects the local settings file.
questions.explain: func azure functionapp fetch-app-settings downloads; func settings encrypt protects.

questions.q: How many triggers can an Azure Function have?

options.why: Correct. Every function has exactly one trigger.
Bindings can be many; triggers can't.
Every function has a trigger.
Learn says exactly one.

questions.hint: Bindings can be many. Triggers can't.
questions.explain: One trigger; zero or more input and output bindings.

questions.q: Each Service Bus message triggers memory-heavy inference, and processing can take 4 minutes. Which host.json settings does Learn recommend tuning?

options.why: maxDeliveryCount is set on the queue resource; 230 s is the HTTP limit.

options.text: authLevel function and concurrency set to 0
options.why: Auth level applies to HTTP triggers.
Correct. One message per instance gets full resources, and lock renewal covers the long call.
High concurrency shares resources across messages.

questions.hint: Heavy messages: process fewer at once, and keep the lock longer than the work.
questions.explain: Tune concurrency and lock renewal for resource-heavy AI processing.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A function calls Azure AI Document Intelligence on every Service Bus message.

rows.text: There's a dedicated Functions binding for Document Intelligence.
rows.why: Services without bindings need SDK clients in code.

rows.text: Creating the client at module level lets it persist across invocations.
DefaultAzureCredential uses the app's managed identity in Azure and developer credentials locally.

questions.hint: No binding exists for every service. Create SDK clients once, outside the handler.
questions.explain: Bindings for supported services; module-level SDK clients for the rest.

questions.q: A production inference endpoint must not be callable anonymously, but full identity checks are handled later by API Management. Which HTTP auth level is the recommended baseline?

options.why: System isn't an HTTP auth level; system keys are for extensions.
Anonymous requires no key.
Correct. Function-level keys are the recommended production baseline.
Admin needs the master key and is for administrative operations.

questions.hint: Keys are a basic barrier. Identity checks come from another layer.
questions.explain: Keys are a basic barrier; layer API Management or Easy Auth for identity.

questions.q: A function app setting uses a Key Vault reference but resolves to an error. The app has a managed identity. What's most likely missing?

options.text: Key Vault Secrets User on the vault
options.why: Correct. Without the role, the runtime can't retrieve the secret.

options.text: A Key Vault binding in function_app.py
options.why: References are resolved by the platform; no binding is needed.

options.text: An App Configuration store for the app
options.why: App Configuration isn't required for Key Vault references.

options.text: A value for the AzureWebJobsStorage setting
options.why: Storage is unrelated to Key Vault resolution.

questions.hint: Key Vault references are resolved by the app's identity. Which data-plane role lets it read values?
questions.explain: Key Vault references need a managed identity with Key Vault Secrets User.

questions.q: Ten function apps and microservices share the same inference threshold and feature flags, which change weekly. Where should these non-secret values live?

options.why: Correct. Change once, and all connected apps get the update.
local.settings.json is for local development only.
host.json is runtime configuration, not shared app settings.

options.text: A Key Vault secret per app
options.why: Key Vault is for secrets.

questions.hint: Shared, non-secret settings that change often belong in a central store.
questions.explain: App Configuration for shared non-secret settings; Key Vault for secrets.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A setting is `@Microsoft.KeyVault(SecretUri=https://myvault.vault.azure.net/secrets/AiServiceKey/)`, with no version.

rows.text: After the secret rotates, the app uses the new version within 24 hours.
rows.why: Versionless URIs pick up new versions within 24 hours.

rows.text: Changing any other app setting forces an immediate refetch.
rows.why: Configuration changes trigger an immediate refetch.

rows.text: The function code must call the Key Vault SDK to read the value.

questions.hint: Versionless URIs follow rotation, and config changes force a refresh.
questions.explain: Use versionless URIs for secrets that rotate on a schedule.

questions.q: A Service Bus trigger uses an identity-based connection named ServiceBusConnection. Which app setting should exist?

options.why: Correct. Messaging services use `__fullyQualifiedNamespace`, e.g. mynamespace.servicebus.windows.net.
`__accountEndpoint` is the Cosmos DB suffix.

options.text: ServiceBusConnection holding a full SAS connection string
options.why: That's a connection string, which identity-based connections replace.
`__accountName` is the storage suffix.

questions.hint: Identity-based connections replace the connection string with the namespace address.
questions.explain: Assign Azure Service Bus Data Receiver to the app's identity.

questions.q: Match each identity-based connection to the role the function app's identity needs.
questions.hint: Each connection needs its own data-plane role.
questions.explain: Each binding extension documents its identity properties and roles.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A function app with identity-based storage uses a **blob trigger** and calls Azure OpenAI.

rows.text: Storage Blob Data Owner alone is enough for the blob trigger.
rows.why: Blob triggers also need Storage Queue Data Contributor and Storage Account Contributor.

rows.text: The identity needs Cognitive Services OpenAI User to call Azure OpenAI.
rows.why: That's the least-privilege role Learn names.

rows.text: Host keys grant access to every HTTP-triggered function in the app.
rows.why: Host keys are scoped to all functions.

rows.text: Function keys verify the caller's Entra ID identity.
rows.why: Keys are a basic barrier; use API Management or Easy Auth for identity.

questions.hint: Blob triggers need more than host storage roles. Keys aren't identity.
questions.explain: Assign least-privilege roles per service; keys aren't identity.

questions.q: A monitoring tool must call every HTTP function in one app, and you want to avoid handing out the master key. Which key type fits?

options.text: Anonymous auth level on every function
options.why: Anonymous removes the key barrier for every caller, not just the tool.
Correct. Host keys cover all functions in the app and suit monitoring agents.
The master key is highly sensitive and grants admin access.
System keys are for extensions, not shared tools.

questions.hint: One key type opens every function in the app without being the master key.
questions.explain: Function keys: one function. Host keys: all functions. Master: admin.

questions.q: A function app uses identity-based `AzureWebJobsStorage__accountName` and has a blob trigger. Which roles does the app identity need on the storage account?

options.text: Storage Blob Data Reader and Storage Queue Data Reader
options.why: Reader roles can't write the receipts and state the trigger needs.

options.text: Storage Account Contributor alone, at subscription scope
options.why: That's a management role. It doesn't give data access, and the scope is too broad.

options.text: Storage Blob Data Owner only, as for host coordination
options.why: That's the minimum for the host. Blob triggers need more.

options.text: Blob Data Owner, Queue Data Contributor, Account Contributor
options.why: Correct. Blob triggers use queues for blob receipts, so they need more than the host's minimum role.

questions.hint: The host needs one role. Blob triggers also use storage queues behind the scenes.
questions.explain: With identity-based AzureWebJobsStorage, the minimum is Storage Blob Data Owner. Blob triggers also need Storage Queue Data Contributor and Storage Account Contributor.

questions.q: Your function app hosts an MCP server through the MCP extension. Which kind of key does the extension use to authenticate MCP client connections?

options.text: The mcp_extension system key that the extension manages
options.why: Correct. Extensions use system keys for internal operations.

options.text: An Entra ID token for each client's user
options.why: Learn names the mcp_extension system key for MCP client connections.

options.text: The master key, shared with every client
options.why: The master key is for administration and should never be handed to clients.

options.text: A function key on each MCP tool function
options.why: Function keys cover one HTTP function. The extension uses its own system key.

questions.hint: Some extensions get their own key type for internal operations.
questions.explain: Key types: function keys (one function), host keys (all functions), the master key (admin), and system keys used by extensions, for example the MCP extension's mcp_extension key.

questions.q: A production inference endpoint must verify each caller's Microsoft Entra identity, not just check for a key. What does Learn recommend layering on top of function keys?

options.why: Admin needs the master key, which is meant for administration.

options.text: An anonymous authorization level with an IP allow list
options.why: Anonymous removes the key barrier, and IP lists don't identify callers.

options.text: A second function key that only trusted callers receive
options.why: More keys are still shared secrets, not identity.

options.text: Azure API Management or Easy Auth
options.why: Correct. Keys are a basic barrier; these add caller identity verification.

questions.hint: Keys say "has the secret". You need "who is calling".
questions.explain: Access keys provide a basic access barrier but don't replace authentication. For caller identity verification, layer Azure API Management or App Service Authentication (Easy Auth).
